items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: This Negro lived in Plaquemine, Louisiana, at the age of about six to eight years old, worked as a shoeshine boy for Ferdinand Herbert, who operated a barbershop in Plaquemine, Louisiana.

ctx.x: This is from Orchestra World. Well, November 1936, letters to the editor. For the record, gentlemen, there is a correction I would like to make in the interview with me appearing in the October issue. In the third paragraph of the article, From Honky Tonk to Swing, I stated that I heard the same tune now called Tiger Rag when I was six or eight years old. Instead of the word same, I meant to say that the tune was somewhat similar to Tiger Rag. Mr. Williams has quoted same, and has put the word same in quotes, and…

Now, I just showed you the kind of propaganda that the people put out. They all knew about Tiger Rag. Now, here's a Negro. I'm going to give you his record. And if I'm wrong, then the world is wrong. This Negro lived in Plaquemine, Louisiana, at the age of about six to eight years old, worked as a shoeshine boy for Ferdinand Herbert, who operated a barbershop in Plaquemine, Louisiana. He came to New Orleans in his late teens. He lies as to hearing Buddy Bowling play. From the dates given in the second line of…

Dear Mr. LaRock, resuming our conversation of last night, I would simply write to repeat. The Marcus of Donegal wrote me and asked me to communicate to you. His address is, the Marcus of Donegal, 16 High Park Gate, London, SWF, England. As you know, Lord Donegal is head of all the jazz clubs of Great Britain. items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: he was a shoeshine boy from a gentleman by the name of Ferdinand, H-E-R-B-E-R-T, Herbert, who ran a barber shop in the city of Plaquemine.

ctx.x: Before who was this came to be?

I mean Clarence Williams. You got me right that time because I'm making a mistake. I'm just telling you, I'm reading. I'm not reading. I'm telling you from my mind. Clarence Williams came to New York around 1923. The first white man he met on Broadway was me with an introduction from A.J. Perron, which you'll find in their books too. And this Negro is supposed to have her buddy bowling play. Now let me tell you about this man, who he is, where he come from. If any of you serious scholars doubt me, I was just…
